query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: When multi‐element, near‐equiatomic nanoparticles are synthesized under conditions that restrict the mobility of reduced metal atoms (e.g., via low‐temperature, solid‐state reduction), a high-entropy, heavily strained solid-solution is kinetically trapped. This state resists atomic rearrangement (such as phase segregation and sintering) at high service temperatures, thus preserving chemical and structural stability during catalytic or thermoelectric operation.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA nanoparticles produced from mixed single-source precursors under low-temperature reduction conditions, exhibiting near-equiatomic, high-entropy mixing and significant lattice strain.
generation.intervention: Prepare two batches of nanoparticles using the same precursor composition: one under conditions that severely restrict atomic mobility (e.g., lower synthesis temperature and rapid cool-down) and a second set processed under conditions that promote greater atomic mobility (e.g., slightly higher synthesis temperature or solvent-assisted mixing).
generation.conditions: Service regimes involving high temperatures (773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications) under inert or controlled atmospheres to mimic operating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The combined effects of high configurational disorder and severe lattice strain which together act as an energetic barrier to atomic diffusion and phase change.
generation.mechanism: Limited diffusion during synthesis freezes the random, high-entropy arrangement of multiple elements and introduces lattice strain. This strain creates additional energy barriers against atom migration. As a result, even under high-temperature service conditions where atomic mobility would normally drive phase segregation or sintering, the nanoparticles remain in a single-phase, disordered state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles synthesized under restricted mobility conditions will maintain a uniform, single-phase structure and stable catalytic or thermoelectric performance after high-temperature exposure, whereas those synthesized with enhanced mobility will show signs of phase segregation, particle coalescence, or degraded functionality.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced by conventional methods without specific control of precursor mobility, which tend to exhibit only moderate thermal stability and may undergo phase changes or sintering at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies primarily when synthesis conditions impose significant kinetic barriers (e.g., rapid cooling or use of solid-state, low temperature reduction) that limit atomic diffusion. It may not hold if the service temperature or duration is sufficient to overcome these barriers, or in synthesis processes where atoms are freely mobile (e.g., in conventional solution-phase syntheses).
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative contribution of lattice strain to the inhibition of atomic diffusion and the interplay with support interactions or specific elemental combinations remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles with identical compositions, varying only the synthesis conditions to modulate precursor mobility (low mobility via lower temperature/rapid quenching vs. higher mobility via elevated temperature or solvent-enhanced mixing). Subject both sets to accelerated thermal aging at 1173 K for a fixed period and then analyze phase composition and particle morphology.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (to detect phase segregation or the emergence of secondary phases)
Transmission electron microscopy (to observe particle coalescence or morphological changes)
Catalytic activity tests (to assess performance changes post aging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If nanoparticles produced under low-mobility synthesis conditions do not exhibit significantly less phase segregation, reduced sintering, and better retention of catalytic/thermoelectric performance compared with the higher-mobility batch after high-temperature treatment, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways.
